## Methods

Biospecimens and quality control
Patients. Biospecimens were collected from five patients diagnosed with prostate cancer as part of the German ICGC cohort. Written informed patient consent and an ethical vote (Institutional Reviewing Board) were obtained according to the ICGC guidelines (see http://www.icgc.org). The local ethics board commission in Hamburg approved the study (PV3552 and PV4679), and the study was conducted following ethical guidelines (Declaration of Helsinki). No statistical methods were used to determine sample sizes since this study was exploratory.

Inclusion criteria were: primary prostate cancers, high-risk, histologically adenocarcinomas, multiple biopsies from a locally advanced specimen with a unifocal disease, and matching pelvic lymph node metastases.

Patients did not receive any neo-adjuvant radiotherapy, ADT, or chemotherapy before the prostatectomy with pelvic lymphadenectomy, except for one patient (ICGC_PCAL25) who received neoadjuvant hormone therapy with LH-RH agonist 6 weeks before surgery. One patient (ICGC_PCAL03) had a known oligometastatic disease stage at the time of operation (M1b stadium in conventional imaging with bone metastases).

All prostate specimens were analyzed according to a standard procedure, including a complete embedding of the entire prostate for histological analysis72. Clinical metadata were retrieved from the patient’s records, and follow-up data were collected with questionnaires.

Pathology review
Specialized pathologists dissected each prostate immediately after surgery as described before27. In brief, dissection followed a pre-defined scheme to represent the position of each block relative to the entire prostate. This procedure resulted in 60–150 pieces of tissues depending on the size of the prostate. After dissection, each tissue block was placed on a separately labeled cork plate covered with a special compound for cryopreservation (OCT) before the tissue was frozen to −20 °C and subsequently stored at −80 °C. Accordingly, the dissection of the lymph node packages proceeded. For each patient, 10 distinct tumor biopsies were taken, and matching lymph node metastases were included in this study (Supplementary Dataset 1). In total, we had a sample collection of 66 samples from 5 different high-risk locally advanced prostate cancer patients (50 primary gland biopsies and 16 matching lymph node biopsies). Gleason grading per individual biopsy was reported (Supplementary Dataset 1). Tumor cell content exceeded 80% for each sample according to pathology reviews.

Sample and library preparation for 10x single-cell multiome ATAC and gene expression
Single-cell sequencing can be prone to batch effects. Given the complexity of our cohort (multiple patients, samples, and tissues), we implemented the following strategy to ensure we are minimizing potential confounding variables of wet-lab library preparation batches and sequencing batches outlined in (Supplementary Dataset 1). Most library-preparation batches (4 samples at a time) incorporated samples from a distinct patient while including randomly chosen samples from another patient. We aimed to randomize samples derived from the same tissue sites across batches as well, such that not all metastatic samples were processed together. This approach was chosen to reduce library preparation batch effects and to better reveal biological variability from technical noise in downstream analyses.

Nuclei isolation
The nuclei were isolated following the adapted protocol for clinically relevant frozen tissues described previously73. We kept the samples on dry ice until use and weighed them individually before starting. The range in weight was between 7 and 24 mg. To perform single-cell multiome ATAC+gene expression analysis, we added 0.2 U/µl of Protector RNAse-Inhibitor (Sigma Aldrich PN-3335399001) to the homogenization buffer (according to the 3’ GEX assay). In brief, we thawed the frozen tissue in a pre-chilled douncer with 1 ml homogenization buffer for 5 min. We then dounced with pestle A for 10 strokes on ice and continued with pestle B for another 10 strokes. We next filtered the solution through a 40 µm tip into a prechilled 1.5 ml Eppendorf tube and spun the nuclei (5 min, 500 × g, 4 °C) in a fixed-angle centrifuge. Then, we removed all but the pellet with 50 µl of supernatant and resuspended it in 350 µl HB to have a total volume of 400 µl. We transferred it to a 2 ml Lo-Bind Eppendorf tube and added 1 volume (400 µl) of 50% iodixanol solution to give a final concentration of 25% iodixanol and mixed by pipetting. Following, we slowly layered 600 µl of 30% iodixanol on top of 600 µl prepared 40% iodixanol and put 800 µl of 25% iodixanol/sample mixture carefully on top. After using a swinging bucket centrifuge (spinning for 20 min at 3000 × g with the brake off), we collected 200 µl of nuclei from the 30%–40% interface into a chilled 1.5 ml tube. We then aliquoted 32,500 nuclei (to aim eventually for 10,000 nuclei) into a 1.5 ml tube. We again spun (10 min, 600 × g, 4 °C) and discarded the supernatant. We next resuspended the pellet in ~6 µl diluted nuclei buffer+RNase inhibitor (see user guide, Chromium Next GEM Single Cell Multiome ATAC+gene expression from 10x).

Library preparation
Single-nucleus libraries were generated using the 10x Chromium single-cell Instrument and Next GEM Single cell multiome ATAC+gene expression kit (10x Genomics) according to the manufacturer’s protocol (Chromium Next GEM single cell multiome ATAC+gene expression Reagent Kits User Guide; CG000338 Rev E). To minimize PCR biases during ATAC library construction, we performed an extra short quantitative PCR (qPCR) to assess how many cycles are needed to amplify our libraries without reaching saturation (1: 72 °C for 5 min, 2: 98 °C for 30 s, 3: 98 °C 10 s, 4: 63 °C for 30 s, 5: 72 °C for 1 min, 6: go to 3–20 times). At the end of the qPCR run, we determined the number of cycles that should be used by looking at the plot of fluorescence vs. the cycle numbers to find out what the maximum fluorescence was, and at what cycle number ¼ of that maximum fluorescence was reached and continued with the ATAC library construction by PCR with 7–9 cycles.

Multiome (snATAC-seq and snRNA-seq) sequencing
Final libraries were quantified using the Qubit dsDNA HS Assay Kit (Life Technologies). The fragment size of every library was analyzed using the Bioanalyzer high-sensitivity chip. All 10x scMultiome ATAC and gene expression libraries were sequenced on the NovaSeq 6000 instruments (Illumina) according to the manufacturer’s protocol (Chromium Next GEM Single Cell Multiome ATAC+gene expression reagent kits user guide; CG000338 Rev E). BCL files were converted into fastq using the command cellranger_arc mkfastq with the default parameter. The generated fastq files were processed using cellranger-arc v2.0.0 count function for read trimming, alignment, duplicate marking (ATAC), and UMI counting (GEX) (Cell Ranger ARC, 10x Genomics). The reads were aligned to the pre-built human reference genome GRCh38—v2020-A-2.0.0 (3 May 2021) provided by 10x Genomics.

Library preparation exclusion criteria and quality control
Nuclei were evaluated after staining with 4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI) and visualized under a high-powered fluorescent microscope (minimum magnification: 40x). Only samples containing high-quality nuclei, defined as clump-free, debris-free, and exhibiting intact membranes, were selected for downstream experimental procedures to ensure data integrity.

After ATAC-library amplification, a quality control (QC) step was performed using qPCR to assess chromatin accessibility. Fold enrichment was calculated by comparing two accessible chromatin regions to two inaccessible chromatin regions. A minimum fold enrichment of 10-fold in accessible regions was required for sample inclusion. The following primer pairs were used:

• Accessible regions (POS).
 ∘ GAPDH: (F) 5′-GCCAATCTCAGTCCCTTCCC-3′, (R) 5’-TAGTAGCCGGGCCCTACTTT-3′
 ∘ KAT6B: (F) 5′-GAAGAGGCGGACCCAGCGGT-3′, (R) 5′-TTCCTGCCGGTCATCTCGCTT-3′

• Inaccessible regions (NEG).
 ∘ SLC22A3: (F) 5′-GGAGAGGGTGGACAGATTGA-3′, (R) 5′-TCAGCCTTGCTGCTACAGTG-3′
 ∘ QML93: (F) 5′-CACTGGTTGTCTTTGCAGGA-3′, (R) 5′-CCTGGGTCATATTGGGACAC-3′

Samples failing to meet these criteria—such as those with poor nuclei integrity or insufficient fold enrichment in accessible over inaccessible chromatin regions—were excluded from further analysis. Therefore following samples were excluded: ICGC_PCAL03_Tu5, ICGC_PCAL03_Tu6, ICGC_PCAL03_Tu8, ICGC_PCAL03_Tu9, ICGC_PCAL10_LN3, ICGC_PCAL10_Tu8, ICGC_PCAL10_Tu9, ICGC_PCAL25_LN1, ICGC_PCAL25_LN2, ICGC_PCAL25_Tu2, ICGC_PCAL25_Tu3, ICGC_PCAL25_Tu4, ICGC_PCAL25_Tu5, ICGC_PCAL25_Tu7, ICGC_PCAL25_Tu9, ICGC_PCAL25_Tu10, ICGC_PCAL34_Tu2, ICGC_PCAL34_Tu3, ICGC_PCAL34_Tu4, ICGC_PCAL34_Tu7, ICGC_PCAL34_Tu10, ICGC_PCAL37_Tu6. Samples with fewer than 1500 cells remaining after cellranger-arc v2.0.0 and QC (described below) were also removed: ICGC_PCAL03_LN2 (838 cells post QC), ICGC_PCAL10_Tu7 (52 cells post QC), ICGC_PCAL10_Tu10 (1339 cells post QC), ICGC_PCAL34_Tu1 (319 cells post QC), ICGC_PCAL37_LN1 (670 cells post QC), ICGC_PCAL37_Tu1 (317 cells post QC). In total, 38 samples (27 individual primary gland tumor biopsies and 11 matching lymph node biopsies) passed all QC criteria for inclusion in the analyses presented in this manuscript (Supplementary Dataset 1 batches and QC).

scMultiome data pre-processing
For each sample, output files from Cell Ranger ARC were processed with Seurat and Signac, with the following versions: R=4.1.0, Signac=1.4.0, Seurat=4.1.0. Cells were filtered if one of the following criteria was met: nFeature_ATAC>500, nFeature_RNA>500, percent.mt<20, TSS.enrichment>2. Cells were removed if both of the following conditions were met: nFeature_RNA>8000 and nFeature_ATAC>80000. Notably, we computed TSS enrichment using the Signac function (TSSEnrichment) and found that median TSS scores reported by ArchR on the same cells are on average, 2.5× higher than those reported by Signac, showcased by recomputing TSS scores using ArchR and Signac across 11 samples from ICGC_PCAL34 (Supplementary Dataset 1). 99% with TSS over 2 in Signac had TSS over 4 using ArchR, and the remaining 1% had a median of Signac TSS 3.6. Lastly, we did not opt for doublet correction and chose to filter on the top percentile of counts for RNA and ATAC, as doublet correction methods on RNA and ATAC individually did not produce results that agreed across samples74,75. Lastly, ATAC data from each sample were then reprocessed using a binned genome approach with 5 kb window sizes across hg38 using the Signac FeatureMatrix function. Downstream analyses were performed on the resulting Seurat object, containing an RNA and tiled genome matrix and were merged across patients.

Inter-patient analysis
Inter-patient data analysis was done using Python (version 3.9.13). Due to the large size of the patient-wide dataset containing all samples, we transitioned from using R to Python-based packages. Subsequent to QC steps and cell filtering described above, Seurat RNA and ATAC assays from each patient were converted to a Python-readable format using R packages MuDataSeurat and SeuratDisk. We then used the Muon package to load and merge each assay across all samples76 and proceeded with downstream processing.

For RNA, we removed mitochondrial and ribosomal transcripts prior to cluster/population calling. We had already used mitochondrial-based metrics to remove low-quality cells. However, mitochondrial and ribosomal reads can represent technical variability unrelated to the biological variability of interest77. Thus, for a more conservative approach in understanding inter-patient heterogeneity, we decided against the inclusion of mitochondrial and ribosomal reads across patients to minimize potential technical variation across patients influencing population-calling (clustering) results. We used scanpy default functions to normalize and scale data (normalize_total), retrieve and highly variable genes (highly_variable_genes), perform dimensionality reduction with PCA, and build the nearest-neighbor graph with defaults.

For ATAC, we normalized with TF-IDF and retrieved the top 5000 highly variable features, performed dimensionality reduction with LSI, and built the nearest neighbor graph on the top 50 LSI dimensions, excluding dimensions with higher than 0.7 Pearson correlation coefficient with depth (nCount_ATAC). We then used the Muon implementation of the weighted-nearest neighbor approach to build an integrated graph of the RNA and ATAC data, which captures the complementary information from both gene expression and chromatin accessibility in each cell28,76. We used Leiden clustering resolution with 1.3 on the obtained multi-modal graph. After clustering, we called peaks for each population using the MACS3 algorithm and built an inter-patient-wide feature set as described below (pseudobulk population calling). We then repeated dimensionality reduction steps for ATAC, recomputed WNN, clustering, and population assignments. Lastly, we did not proceed with batch correction, as nonmalignant cell populations showed inter-mixing across patients. This is indicative of the clustering algorithms preserving genuine biological differences. Batch correction could be potentially detrimental to removing meaningful differences across malignant epithelial populations78.

Intra-patient analyses
All intra-patient analyses were performed in R version=4.1.0, Signac=1.4.0, and Seurat=4.1.0. For prostate-specific analyses (Fig. 2), we merged samples coming from the primary tumor sections within a prostate gland of a given patient. For intra-patient analyses across tissues (Fig. 4), we merged all samples from metastatic lymph nodes and primary prostate tumor sections. For each merged object, we processed RNA, ATAC, and the subsequent Multiome object as described above, but used the equivalent R-based Seurat/Signac implementations. For RNA processing, we used SCTransform to normalize the filtered count matrix and PCA to run louvain graph-based clustering on the first 50 principal components, and for ATAC, we used RunTFIDF to normalize the data, found highly variable regions using FindTopFeatures, and RunSVD to project ATAC data to lower dimensions. We built the nearest neighbor graph on the top 50 PCA and top 50 LSI dimensions, excluding dimensions with higher than 0.7 correlation with ATAC depth (ATAC_nCount). The weighted nearest neighbor graph was built using FindMultiModalNeighbors. Populations were called on this graph using FindClusters for each patient with multiple resolutions, we tested and annotated clusters across resolutions 0.4, 0.6, and 0.8; and found 0.4 to cover the major cell types across all patients.

Pseudobulk peak calling
We wrote a Snakemake pipeline for calling and merging peaks for any group of cells in our dataset. First, we generated a fragment TSV file for every cell in a given group (in this case, our called populations) per sample. Second, MACS3 was then used to call peaks on the fragment files with the following parameters: -f BED -q 0.01 -g 2.7e9 --keep-dup all --nomodel --nolambda --shift −75 --extsize 150 --bdg --call-summits79 and peaks were iteratively merged80. We then re-computed the FeatureMatrix in Signac and either transferred to Python for inter-patient analysis or added them to the Seurat objects for intra-glandular/intra-patient analyses. Third, the new FeatureMatrices were used to obtain signal over promoter and non-promoter elements and compute ChromVar-based transcription factor enrichment scores29. For each peak catalog, we assigned whether a peak was a promoter element if it was within +−1 kb TSS in gene code transcript annotations, otherwise, the peak was annotated as non-promoter, which was used in subsequent Pearson correlation analyses described below. We used a merged peakset across all samples for inter-patient and patient-specific peaksets for intra-patient analyses.

Population annotations
We used a multi-faceted manual and automated approach to go about population annotations, independently utilizing RNA and ATAC data. For every population, we computed the marker genes and chromVar transcription factor motif enrichments by looking at the top upregulated genes relative to the entire sample of interest (Seurat’s FindAllMarkers). For every cell in our dataset, we computed the singleR assignments using the publicly available default datasets and a prostate-specific dataset81,82. We also computed each cell’s ModuleScore across gene expression markers reported in relevant papers24,82–84 using Seurat’s AddModuleScore, with additional cell-cycle markers obtained from https://github.com/hbc/tinyatlas. We then visualized all singleR’s cell type assignment proportions per population and visualized ModuleScores to facilitate manual cell type assignments. For every population, we checked the alignment of the highly expressed genes with expected genes per cell type with literature search and available atlases (protein atlas.org). We also utilized ATAC-based transcription factor-deviation scores per population, as ATAC signal tends to be less prone to biological variability such as cell cycle, and TF-motif enrichment computations rely on more global genome-wide statistics. We cross-referenced TFs based on their enrichment relative to the expected average (which would contain more malignant epithelial cell TFs) and annotated populations according to TFs. Furthermore, more than one expert was exposed to the population markers and visualizations and independently annotated populations according to the steps above to ensure agreement. This rigorous, multi-layered approach provided confidence that our findings represent biological cell types within and across patient samples.

Assessing the degree of phenotypic heterogeneity in locus-specific populations
We assessed heterogeneity between populations in two ways. First, we reported how inter-mixed populations were based on variables of interest, such as patient, tumor locus, and tissue, using Shannon entropy. Additionally, to compare scores across patients when reporting the median across patients, we normalized the scores to be between 0 and 1 when 0 indicating no entropy and 1 indicating maximum entropy relative that can be achieved given the number of loci and cells per loci. Second, we derived Pearson correlation values on DESeq2 normalized pseudobulked signal across the three feature sets of non-promoter DNA elements, as well as promoter elements and gene expression. We obtained normalized pseudobulked values per population by summing raw counts of each population according to the three feature sets and normalizing them using DESeq2 vst85. To assess how transcription factor families drive variance, we conducted PCA on median chromVar motif deviations per population. We then binned the feature loadings into 30 bins across 633 motifs, covering the top and bottom ~5th percentiles of features contributing to a given axis of variation.

To contextualize biological programmes driving intra-prostate tumor heterogeneity, we used the SCENIC+ pipeline on tumors from ICGC_PCAL34 and ICGC_PCAL0337. Pre-processing of ATAC data for the SCENIC+ pipeline was done using the polars_1xx branch of the pycisTopic package for scalability purposes. ScRNA preprocessing and the SCENIC+ pipeline were run according to recommendations highlighted at https://scenicplus.readthedocs.io/en/latest/. eRegulon specificity scores for each malignant epithelial cluster were calculated using sceniecplus.RSS.regulon_specificity_scores() to select the top 10 most specific and confident eRegulons per malignant epithelial cluster. The genes of the highly specific eRegulons were used to create gene lists for pathway enrichment using the gseapy Python package.

CNV inference
We used the NUMBAT algorithm39,86 to perform CNV inference. We performed NUMBAT per sample to ensure tumor vs. normal calls were properly cross-referenced with our RNA/ATAC-based cell type annotations. We then used NUMBAT on a patient-wide basis to get a sense of all CNV segments with higher accuracy. However, due to the large number of cells from each patient, we kept only the cells annotated as malignant epithelial and had to further subsample the number of cells used in the per-patient analysis as follows, for the pipeline to run. To allow computational feasibility, we kept a maximum of 3000 cells per sample in ICGC_PCAL03, ICGC_PCAL10, ICGC_PCAL37, and 6000 malignant epithelial cells per sample in ICGC_PCAL34 and ICGC_PCAL25. Lymphocyte populations from ICGC_PCAL10 and ICGC_PCAL37 were used as background, since they had the largest number of cells from the TME. For visualization purposes (Fig. 2b), we used the most common CNV call in all cells assigned to a given clone. To compute the difference between clones, we used the Hamming metric, which measures the distance between two vectors of equal length. The CNV calls per cell were then used to compute this metric between all cells and clones, to broadly assess the difference between clones in a given patient.

Assessing the degree of clonal architecture heterogeneity in populations
We assessed how similar the clonal makeup of each population was according to the Jensen–Shannon (JS) divergence metric. We used JS divergence as it provides a symmetrical and finite measurement of the difference between two probability distributions. For every malignant epithelial population with more than 200 cells, we computed the proportion of cells that were assigned to each clone, and the JS distance was calculated per population pairs.

Differentially accessible regions and transcripts identification and analyses
To identify differentially accessible peaks and transcripts, we pseudobulked raw counts from malignant cells from a given patient per sample across all features. Only cells annotated as malignant epithelial were kept. We then used DESeq2’s ~patient+tissue to retrieve differential peaks and transcripts of primary prostate and metastatic lymph nodes, FDR thresholded at <0.1. We then computed transcription factor DNA motif enrichment scores using HOMER on differentially accessible peaks with absolute LFC > 1 and q < 0.187.

Ambient RNA correction
To gain confidence in our differential analyses, we repeated our pipeline but used ambient RNA corrected count matrices using CellBender43. We optimized parameters per sample, except for the FPR, which we had to keep consistent across all, according to the authors (FPR=0.05). Overall, CellBender retained a median of 40% more cells than Cell Ranger and did not have an apparent benefit to the malignant epithelial cell expression patterns (Supplementary Fig. 8a, b). We kept only the cells that passed QC according to our scMultiome data pre-processing as outlined, and repeated our differential analysis as described above.

Validation of gene signatures in an external single-cell RNA seq dataset
To validate the AUCell enrichment scores of gene signatures, we utilized an external dataset47. Specifically, we downloaded the Seurat eRegulons object (primecut.integrated.geneexp.seurat.rds) from the publicly available repository hosted at https://data.mendeley.com/datasets/5nnw8xrh5m/1. This dataset contains gene expression profiles of castration-sensitive prostate cancer (mCSP) cells from various metastatic sites. We subset the dataset to exclude TME cell types, isolating a total of 3976 malignant epithelial mCSPC cells. These cells were distributed across four metastatic sites: lymph nodes (n=1096), bone (n=1263), lung (n=641), and liver (n=976). We calculated AUCell enrichment scores for our lymph node up- and down-regulated genes across the treatment stages in all metastatic sites to assess the dynamics of our gene signatures in response to treatment. We calculated AUCell enrichment scores for lymph node up- and down-regulated genes across treatment stages in all metastatic sites to assess gene signature dynamics. Scores were normalized between 0 and 1, and a Kruskal–Wallis test determined whether at least one treatment group differed significantly. Pairwise comparisons were conducted using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test. This approach allowed us to investigate both site-specific and systemic changes in gene signature dynamics during mCSPC progression and treatment.

Non-genetic yet inheritable drivers of phenotypic heterogeneity are well established in developmental biology and gaining recognition in cancer 2,3. Specifically, differentiating cells arise from the acquisition of epigenomic variation, such as changes in chromatin accessibility, over narrow (~500bp) genomic loci 4. In this manuscript, phenotypic heterogeneity is evident in both chromatin accessibility and transcriptional profiles. Specifically, the cluster-calling algorithm integrates both mRNA expression and chromatin accessibility data to construct a graph of cellular relationships 7, leveraging the complementary information from these modalities to define cell populations.

We acknowledge the importance of accurate CNV inference and thank them for pointing out ambiguities in the methods section. Numbat automatically chooses the background based on the correlation of supplied pseudobulked background cells with individual malignant epithelial cells. We have revised our sentence in the manuscript for clarification (Methods: CNV Inference page 22, line 2). Our rationale for subsampling was motivated both by computational feasibility and statistical considerations.
Subsampling was necessary due to R’s memory ceiling, as Numbat computes a pairwise distance matrix (ape::nj) which grows quadratically with the number of supplied cells, and we found the limit to be around ~35,000 cells. We estimated the maximum number of cells which enables computational feasibility of per-patient CNV inference to be 3,000, with each run taking ~1TB of RAM and ~7-10 days to complete depending on the patient. Thus, higher input sizes were not feasible for per-patient runs. Furthermore, we reasoned that for each patient’s CNV inference, would mitigate the risk of overfitting clonal inference to any one spatial location by subsampling the number of cells obtained from each region to roughly an equal number. Finally, in response to the reviewer’s request and technical considerations, we showcase results for ICGC_PCAL34 when subsampling to a maximum of 3,000 versus 6,000 cells per spatial region. We found little difference in segment detection between the two runs, with 93% of basepairs detected as segments in the 6,000 cells per region run are detected as segments in the 3,000 cells per region run (Rebuttal Figure 2.1A). We then computed the weighted hamming distance of CNV labels between cells, which represents the difference between CNV segment calls between 6,000 versus 3,000 across the genome weighted by the length of the CNV ranging from 0 to 1. 0 implies no difference in CNV labels and 1 implies all CNV labels differing in the 3,000 cell from 6,000 cell run. Each CNV segment is weighted by its length in basepairs divided by total number of basepairs covered by all segments called in the larger 6,000 cells/region run. We saw a median hamming distance of 0.1 across shared (N=15,000) cells, indicating little difference across the called CNV segments (Rebuttal Figure 2.1B). We have now included segment calls on the single cell level in Supplementary Figure 5B.

Other definitions of plasticity have been suggested to distinguish microenvironmental and cell-intrinsic sources of heterogeneity according to phenotypic read-outs 3, and we have now contextualized our findings accordingly in the discussion section (page 12, lines 26-38).
Our intention in generating this dataset was to clarify how single-cell-based populations could be utilized for identifying common ancestors that may exhibit migration capabilities. We considered methods for population tracking and found the CNV-based approach applied in our manuscript to be the most technically-sound.
However, inferred CNVs did not support a genetic (i.e.: clonal) history between regions, which led us to focus on expanding our study to the phenotypic comparisons between lymph nodes and primary tumors.
We agree with the reviewer on the value of placing cells on a timeline, and explain our rationale for excluding pseudotime or velocity-based approaches from the main figures below:
1. Algorithmic ancestral relationships identification (pseudotime and velocity-based approaches): Population dynamics of single cells can be modelled using velocity-based algorithms, which rely on the observed shifts in intronic and exonic read ratios. While we implemented this approach in our dataset, we found that it was not an ideal method for solid tumor samples. These methods assume relatively uniform transcriptional dynamics and consistent splicing behavior across cells and would be correctly utilized for single-sample analysis. We must note that velocity-based approaches, or other graph-based algorithms, can be sound and useful for more well-defined systems of development combined with more reductive/controlled models with well-known directional patterns in cell fate, where the entire space of intermediate cell states are captured within a single experiment 16,17. However, the assumptions made by these algorithms are often not met in tumor tissues and are exacerbated by pre-processing of multiple samples, which leads to distortions in algorithmic inference of trajectories 18. This is especially prominent in velocity algorithms, which are unsuitable for our complex multi-sampled cohort.
Lastly, in cancer settings, single-cell sequencing provides a snapshot of phenotypic behavior during the time of surgery. Algorithmic inference of trajectories using graph-based models requires a knowledge of directionality and sufficient similarity between populations to avoid false positives. This is complex in the case of cancer. For example, in normal development, well-researched stemness markers can be used for guidance in assessing directionality and avoiding false-positives. Whereas in cancer settings they may represent progenitor populations 20,21 or growing daughter cells as a result of cancer progression 22. Thus, in the case of our cohort, we found identifying ancestral relationships and population dynamics using the available phenotype-based algorithms to be unsuitable for defining the relationship between malignant populations.
While acknowledging these limitations, we performed pseudotime analysis on one patient ICGC_PCAL34, with four tumour regions and a single lymph node, presents the simplest case in our cohort for defining trajectories using Monocle3 19. We used Monocle3 to preprocess the data subsetted on all cells belonging to malignant epithelial clusters (Rebuttal Figure 2.3 A). We observed partitioning to resemble inter-loci heterogeneity, where the best possible path between cell states are localized to single loci, with the exception of Tu5 and Tu8. While relaxing partitioning by Monocle3 can reveal continuous paths between sampled regions (Rebuttal Figure 2.3 B-C), it can lead to spurious paths that may not be representative of the biological differentiation path and is not recommended practice. Thus, pseudotime analysis is constrained by patient-specific inter-loci phenotypic states rather than inter-loci transitions. Additionally, the Monocle-based graph and called populations were similar to those already captured by the weighted nearest neighbor graph-derived populations, underscoring the robustness of our integrated clustering approach (Rebuttal Figure 2.3 D-E).
2. Copy number variation(CNV)-based approaches: Our intention for incorporating CNVs was to (i) more confidently annotate populations and (ii) utilize CNVs as surrogates for lineage tracing in our single-cell sequencing analysis as CNVs have been used to track evolution in cancer progression 23 and address the complexities of tumor heterogeneity, which render the methods above unsuitable. While we initially utilized the CNV-based approach to identify and isolate malignant populations in the prostate with migration capabilities to the lymph nodes, our findings suggested a more homogeneous clonal architecture among the malignant epithelial populations, an observation which we elaborated in our paper. Thus, we could not confidently place subclones on a genetic timeline representing the seeding to the lymph nodes. This underscored that there may be phenotypic changes that occur without detectable clonal divergence in CNV-based markers, so we turned to primary and metastatic comparisons.

Thus, we are not able to derive a relationship between phenotypic and genotypic diversity and physical proximity. However, we observed that, with the exception of patient ICGC_PCAL34, lymph node samples exhibited similar clonal architecture both to one another and to their matched primary tumors. In contrast, some intraglandular clones, such as clone 3 in ICGC_PCAL10, were restricted to specific regions of the primary tumor and not detected in any lymph nodes, suggesting their limited dissemination (Figure 4B, Supplementary Figure 5). These findings indicate that major clones can disseminate across lymph nodes, while some subclones remain confined to specific primary tumor regions. We cannot exclude the possibility of spatially proximal regions of the prostate tumors disseminating to the lymph node which may share a similar clonal architecture to our sampled regions.
The number of cells retrieved per locus is summarized in Table 1 ("batches_qc"), which also provides an overview of sampling depth across primary and metastatic sites (Methods: Sample and library preparation for 10x single-cell multiome ATAC and gene expression).
Regarding whether the co-annotated TME cell types may influence colonization of the Lymphnode: while the majority of cells in our dataset are malignant epithelial cells (see response to C1.1), we do detect a range of TME cell types. However, as noted in our response to comment C1.1, the limited sample size and proportion of non-malignant cells precludes a robust investigation of specific TME-malignant crosstalk axes (e.g., fibroblast-epithelial interactions). We have further clarified this point in the discussion (Page 11, lines 6-20): “Phenotypic heterogeneity in malignant cells, both between and within patients, suggests that primary tumor formation is shaped by patient-specific tumor evolutionary processes. In contrast, TME cell types, such as immune and stromal cells, are relatively conserved across patients. The similarity in TME composition aligns with prior single-cell studies for other malignancies 49–51 and supports targeting the TME as an alternative therapeutic strategy in high-risk prostate cancer 52. While our Shannon entropy analysis revealed relative conservation of TME composition across patients and spatial sites, it does not preclude the possibility that local, spatially restricted interactions contribute to phenotypic heterogeneity between malignant populations 53–55. Whether TME and malignant epithelial populations with similar phenotypes congregate in distinct spatial pockets 54,55 and if local cellular interactions result in genetically distinct cells to adopt shared phenotypes remain to be explored. Addressing these will require a different setup, such as high-resolution spatial sequencing technologies, to more precisely map the interplay between the TME and malignant populations.”
Rebuttal Figure 3.3 (New Supplementary Figure 2): Detailed pathology map of biopsied regions within the primary tumor. Annotated pathology map displaying the precise localization of all biopsied regions within the primary prostate tumor. A comprehensive description of the pathology review and region annotation criteria is provided in the Methods section (Pathology Review), and detailed histomorphological features, including Gleason scores for each region, are provided in Table 1
C3.4. Most of the patients analyzed had tumor specimens from multiple cores of the prostate and from the Lymphnodes but the analysis does not provide any hint on how prostate cancer cells seem to metastasize. The results could be masked by the fact that several sites in the primary tumors are taken into account in the analysis. Can the author perform the analysis taking the prostate cores and each LN site separately? Can the author infer that high “phenotypic” plasticity can be an account for, or evidence of monoclonal spreading and seeding ?
Our analysis was performed at the individual sample level, that is, each regionally distinct sample was used to prepare the single-cell sequencing library independently. This design allows us to preserve and investigate site-specific variation in both clonal and phenotypic composition. In Supplementary Figure 5, we show per-sample pie charts depicting the distribution of genotypically inferred clones across each primary tumor locus and matched LN metastasis. To improve clarity, we have now revised the figure legend to read: “Pie charts depicting distribution of separately inferred genotypic clones for cells coming from each primary tumor loci and each matched lymph node metastases per patient.”
Since the clonal architecture in LN metastases generally resembled that of the primary tumors, it suggested that multiple clones can seed and survive dissemination without undergoing a strong evolutionary bottleneck from a genetic perspective. This is consistent with previous findings from bulk sequencing 24–26. Thus, we sought out to identify common phenotypic shifts that may be shared across patients by considering data from all patients. This reinforces a role for non-genetic mechanisms, such as epigenetic variation, to support phenotypic plasticity for cancer cells to survive in changing environments and tissues. These observations are consistent with DNA barcode-based lineage tracing studies 27–2927,2829, which have shown that prostate cancer cells can undergo common phenotypic transitions under metastatic and therapeutic pressure without clonal selection. (Manuscript: page 11 lines 21-37: “Despite phenotypic and genotypic inter-patient variability, we found that a common phenotypic shift occurs in malignant epithelial cells disseminating to the lymph nodes across patients. The clonal architecture in lymph node metastatic cancer cells resembled that of the malignant epithelial cells in primary tumor loci in each patient. This suggests that clones can seed and survive the dissemination process in lymph nodes without undergoing an evolutionary bottleneck based on their CNV composition, consistent with bulk sample genetic sequencing studies 4,6,56. Additionally, barcode-based studies support a model of tumor evolution relying on phenotypic plasticity57,58. For instance, individual malignant prostate cancer cells, tagged with unique DNA barcodes, were shown to withstand selective pressures, such as metastatic dissemination and treatment resistance, by undergoing phenotypic transitions 59. While paired deep whole-genome sequencing data may reveal rare mutations that could impact phenotypic transitions, our observations support a contribution for non-genetic variation, including changes in chromatin accessibility in non-coding DNA elements, in defining the phenotype of disseminating malignant epithelial cells adapted to survive in sites beyond the primary tumor.”
C3.5. Why AR and other TFs e.g. FOXA1 TFs were not enriched in the tumor cells in the Lymphnodes compared to primary regions?
Figure 4 represents transcription factor motif enrichment within differentially accessible chromatin between primary and lymph node sites. AR (NR) family and FOXA1 (Forkhead family) are still detected as enriched factors (Figure 4F). Our findings imply increased accessibility around motifs of immune-based transcription factors such as the ETS family, rather than the lack of AR signalling in malignant cells in the LN. This also supports the differential transcriptional programs observed with RNA (Figure 4E).
Given that AR and FOXA1 are still observed in LN cells, our findings reflect an increase in immune-signalling co-occurring with continued reliance on AR as the core driver of prostate cancer. (Manuscript: page 12 lines 3-7 “Our investigation revealed phenotypic plasticity between primary and metastatic lymph node malignant cells were marked by a transition from prostate-specific pathways to immune/inflammatory-like states within the cancer cells themselves, suggesting engagement of epithelial-intrinsic immune programs during dissemination. ”)
C3.6. The reviewer understands that the 4/5 patients were treatment näive but one of them was ADT pretreated. Is there any noticable difference between the tumor cells retrieved in this ADT treated patient lymphnodes compared to the tumor cells retrieved from the lymph nodes of the other treatment näive patients?
We thank the reviewer for this important question. Indeed, among the five patients in our cohort, one had received short-course neoadjuvant ADT prior to surgery. We agree that comparing the lymph node metastases from this patient to those from treatment-naïve individuals would be highly informative in understanding treatment-related effects on tumor phenotypes and clonal dynamics. While lymph node tissue was available for this ADT-treated patient, the nuclei isolation procedure unfortunately yielded insufficient quality for downstream single-cell profiling. As a result, only the primary tumor samples from this case were included in the current single-cell analysis. Therefore, our present dataset does not support a direct comparison of lymph node metastases between treatment-naïve and ADT-pretreated patients. (Manuscript Page 10 lines 22-26: “Our own cohort precluded contextualizing these gene sets with respect to drug treatment, as the only androgen deprivation therapy (ADT)-treated patient (ICGC_PCAL25), the LN samples had insufficient quality for downstream single-cell profiling. Thus, we turned to external single-cell RNA sequencing data from metastatic prostate cancer 48. [...]”
C3.7. The authors focus their analysis on the epithelial-like cells but other cell types present in the specimens seem to be ignored. In light of the tumor (immune) microenvironment shaping the metastatic potential, can the author distinguish more immune active vs colder tumors and foci and their propensity and features leading to tumor cell dissemination? Are these just simply the result of higher inflammation on the primary site?
Recent studies have classified tumors into immune “hot” versus “cold” states based on T cell infiltration, PD-L1 (CD274) expression, and tumor mutational burden (TMB) 30. Prostate cancer is considered an immune-cold tumor type 31, and this is supported by our own single-cell data, where T cells constituted only ~1.95% of all profiled cells, limiting robust T cell-based stratification across patients. With this caveat in mind, we decided to assess CD274 (PD-L1) expression within malignant epithelial cells across tumor and lymph node (LN) foci. Gene expression was log-normalized using the LogNormalize method in Seurat before visualization. Overall, CD274 expression was low across all sites from all patients (Rebuttal Figure 3.7A), consistent with the immune-cold phenotype of prostate cancer.
Rebuttal Figure 3.7: PD-L1 (CD274) expression across tumor loci. Violin plots displaying the mean log-normalized expression of PD-L1 (CD274) across all tumor loci for each individual patient.

Reviewer #4, expertise in prostate cancer epigenetics and mechanisms of lineage plasticity (Remarks to the Author):
In this manuscript, Keshavarzian et al employs scMultiome to dissect intra- and inter-tumoral heterogeneity in high-risk prostate cancer across spatially distinct primary tumor loci and matched locoregional lymph node (LN) metastases. This research show that Inter-patient heterogeneity is largely restricted to malignant epithelial cells and LN metastases mirror the clonal diversity of primary tumors but undergo a transcriptional shift toward inflammatory-like states. This work advances the understanding of prostate cancer progression by linking clonal architecture to phenotypic plasticity. The inflammatory transition paradigm also provides a framework for targeting non-genetic adaptation mechanisms in metastasis. The following points need to be considered.
Major comments:
C4.1. The cohort size and clinical annotation are limited in this study which includes only 5 patients, with one receiving neoadjuvant therapy. The author can explicitly discuss how cohort size limits statistical power for inter-patient comparisons and include clinical outcomes (e.g., recurrence, survival) if available to contextualize the observed heterogeneity.
While this study was designed as an in-depth exploratory analysis of spatial heterogeneity using single-cell multiomic profiling in a rare and clinically relevant setting (paired primary and locoregional metastatic tissues from high-risk prostate cancer patients), we agree that a larger cohort size would have been beneficial. Our current cohort includes five patients, the extensive spatial sampling per patient (up to 10 biopsies per individual) and the high resolution of ~300,000 single-nucleus profiles which enabled robust intra-patient comparisons and allowed us to identify conserved phenotypic trends across patients despite inter-individual variation.
Nonetheless, we acknowledge that the small number of patients limits the statistical generalizability of inter-patient comparisons. We now explicitly discuss this limitation in the revised Discussion section and caution against over-interpreting patient-specific findings as broadly representative. Clinical annotations, such as histopathologic features (e.g., Gleason score), were leveraged to contextualize some findings, such as ICGC_PCAL37 in the Results Section “Malignant cells disseminating to locoregional lymph nodes undergo an inflammatory-like cell state transition despite genotypic similarity to primary cancer”; page 9 lines 3-8 and page 10 lines 7-10. Our cohort, which is limited in size and restricted to lymph node metastasis, constraints our ability to expand our findings to distal metastases and contextualize clinical outcomes.
We agree that future studies with larger cohorts and longitudinal follow-up data will be essential to link the observed cellular heterogeneity to patient outcomes and treatment response (raised on page 12, lines 21-25)
C4.2. ICGC_PCAL37, which has the lowest Gleason score, has some specificity in some aspect, such as lower tumor heterogeneity and the unique inter-site difference. These may indicate that the stage of tumor progression can have an impact on the inter- and intra-tumor heterogeneity. The author can discuss how tumor progression relates to the heterogeneity of prostate tumor inter- and intra-site through the analysis of wider range of statistic data from their own or in the public database
Extensive prior work has shown that prostate cancer displays marked inter-patient heterogeneity across histo-morphological and molecular dimensions in both primary and metastatic disease settings 32–37. Large-scale genomic studies have further delineated molecular subtypes of prostate cancer that differ at the genetic level despite sharing similar histopathological grades 38–44.
In our cohort, patient ICGC_PCAL37, the only case with a Gleason score of 7 (3+4), stood out in several respects. This individual exhibited comparatively lower tumor heterogeneity and unique inter-site differences. Clinically, this patient had no evidence of bone metastases (similar to ICGC_PCAL10), experienced biochemical recurrence relatively early, and remained stable for an extended period following salvage radiation therapy before initiating systemic treatment nearly five years later (Table 1: baseline_metadata, therapy_follow_up). These characteristics may reflect a more indolent disease course and support the idea that earlier-stage tumors may harbor lower levels of molecular heterogeneity.
While our dataset includes only five patients, limiting the statistical power to formally compare Gleason score with heterogeneity metrics, previous studies support this link. For example, high-risk prostate cancers with elevated Gleason scores tend to exhibit more pronounced somatic copy number alterations (SCNAs) and greater genomic instability 45, Figure 2). Similarly, The Cancer Genome Atlas44 reported that tumors with high SCNA burden are associated with higher Gleason scores and elevated PSA levels (Figures S3B–S3D).
Furthermore, the degree of structural rearrangement has been shown to increase across Gleason grades: tumors with any Gleason pattern 4 component (e.g., 3+4 or 4+3) demonstrate significantly higher rearrangement rates than Gleason 3+3 tumors 44, Figure 1). These studies collectively support the hypothesis that tumor progression correlates with increasing inter- and intra-tumor heterogeneity.
C4.3. Bone metastases are very common in prostate cancer. Does prostate bone metastases also show an immune/inflammatory-like states transition similar with LN metastases? The author can discuss the potential universality of this inflammatory-like states.
As our cohort includes only lymph node metastases, we are unable to directly assess whether bone metastases exhibit a similar immune/inflammatory-like state transition. However, prior work by others 46 has examined progression biopsies from mCRPC patients, including bone metastases, and similarly reported enrichment of immune/inflammatory-related pathways, such as interferon signaling and IL6/JAK/STAT—during treatment resistance. This suggests that such inflammatory-like states may represent a shared, site-independent mechanism associated with lineage plasticity. While distant metastatic organs such as bone and liver are considered aggressive metastatic disease, locoregional lymph nodes may similarly capture this evolving aggressive biology due to ongoing clonal seeding from the primary site prior to therapy 24. Thus, although our analysis is limited to lymph node metastases, the inflammatory-like transcriptional states we observe may reflect a generalizable mechanism of metastatic adaptation and resistance. sWe have added a brief statement in the Discussion to reflect this point (page 12, lines 3-14): “These immune/inflammatory-like pathways, including JAK-STAT signaling, have also been observed in mCRPC progression samples across diverse metastatic sites, including bone 63. JAK-STAT signalling is also implicated as a driver of plasticity and dedifferentiation from luminal-epithelial cell states in prostate cancer models 64,65. This suggests that activation of these pathways may represent a mechanism of progression and potentially contribute to treatment resistance, though this hypothesis warrants further validation. ”
Lastly, we used our chromatin variants to get their global enrichment over mCRPC bone metastases profiled using bulk ATAC-sequencing. We observed the primary Tu chromatin variants to score lower than the LN chromatin variants (Wilcoxon P=0.008), with respect to the average chromatin accessibility profile across mCPRC samples. However, these samples were profiled using bulk ATAC-sequencing which implies that the computed signal is inclusive of cells in the tumor microenvironment. For this reason, we turned to performing the same analyses on over prostate cancer cell lines which are composed of purely malignant cells. We saw that LN chromatin variants were more enriched in aggressive cell lines (PC3s and Du145, Wilcoxon P=0.029) relative to Tu chromatin variants which were more pronounced in less aggressive hormone dependent cell lines (LNCaP, 22RV1, VCaPs, Wilcoxon P=0.008).
Rebuttal 4.3 LN chromatin variant signatures are more enriched relative to primary Tu in aggressive prostate cancers. A) Chromatin variant enrichments in 28 bulk ATAC-seq mCRPC bone metastasis samples. Enrichment scores computed using ChromVar, which assesses the relative enrichment of all differential LN (N=5544, Log Fold Change > 0.5, adjusted P-val < 0.1) and Tu (N=5312, Log Fold Change > 0.5, adjusted P-val < 0.1) peaks on a consensus mCRPRC peakset. B) Chromatin variant enrichments computed in a similar manner on a consensus cell line peakset, with two replicates per cell line with the exception of VCaPs. C) Depiction of individual cell line data and replicates in (B) as a heatmap, color-scale is limited to a minimum and maximum of -10 and +10 Z-scores.
C4.4. While the transcriptional shifts in LN metastases are compelling, the functional consequences of inflammatory reprogramming remain speculative. In vitro assays (e.g., cytokine exposure) or spatial proteomics could help in validating inflammatory signatures as well as the cellular function of this transition.
While the functional consequences of inflammatory reprogramming remain to be fully elucidated, we partially addressed this by validating our lymph node (LN)-upregulated transcriptional signature using an independent single-cell RNA-seq dataset from metastatic prostate cancer across treatment stages 47. We observed an enrichment of LN-up genes during disease progression and treatment resistance (Figure 4g), supporting their biological relevance. Similar pathways were also shown to be upregulated in mCRPC progression post-Enzalutamide treatment 46, and aggressive prostate cancer cells expressing immune-like markers were previously observed in mouse models 48.
We agree that spatial transcriptomic and proteomic technologies could provide further insight into the local context and function of these states. Similarly recent technological advances, such as spatial scATAC-seq and in situ tagmentation, highlight promising future directions for dissecting spatial epigenomic heterogeneity 49,50.We believe our findings help lay the groundwork for such future studies.
We also acknowledge the potential value of in vitro cytokine exposure assays to interrogate the functional consequences of inflammatory reprogramming. However, given the broad scope of our transcriptional signatures, encompassing multiple pathways and hundreds of genes, designing targeted perturbation experiments would require substantial additional work to deconvolute pathway-specific effects. As with IHC-based validation, these experiments, while valuable, fall beyond the scope of the current study.
C4.5. In this research, sampling focuses on primary tumors and LN metastases but lacks the adjacent normal tissue comparisons to define tumor-specific changes. Spatial transcriptomics may help in mapping phenotypic transitions at the invasion front.
While our manuscript was focused on investigating the primary and metastatic heterogeneity, we did not have access to matched adjacent normals to define tumor-specific changes. However, we utilized the identified tumor-microenvironment cell types as a reference point as discussed in our response to comment C2.7. We have additionally covered how our data highlights spatial transcriptomics to be imperative to our understanding of prostate cancer heterogeneity and metastasis (See response to comment C1.2 and revised Discussion page 11 line 6-20)

C4.6. In line 335, the author claims that “lymph node-specific malignant epithelial populations consistently ranked higher than primary tumor-specific malignant epithelial populations across all patients”. However, in ICGC_PCAL37 the rank of the two population looks the same.
Patient ICGC_PCAL37 had the most inter-mixing across sites, with a single lymph-node specific malignant epithelial population (as reported in Results page 9 lines 3-8), hence, as the reviewer points out, we were not able to draw strong conclusions from this patient. Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
Authors have partially addressed my concerns related to the manuscript. Still major issues remain.
1. For CNV analysis authors could consider more optimized (e.g. python) implementation of the algorithms. None of the less, authors do demonstrate data to alleviate concern regarding subsampling. However, how the choice of reference cell type impacts the CNV calls has not been properly addressed. As different cell types expressed different set of genes this can have fundamental impact on inferred CNVs and thus on conclusions.
Response: We agree with the reviewer that the majority of CNV calling algorithms are based solely on RNA expression and are therefore sensitive to the choice of reference. We did not experience this to be a problem for Numbat because it relies on both haplotype frequency (reference-independent) and molecular abundance (reference-dependent).
To this point, a very recent CNV-calling benchmarking paper showcases that with the exception of Numbat, most other CNV callers are sensitive to the choice of reference (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-62359-9). This paper demonstrated Numbat’s high performance in
1. Outperforming all other methods at detecting the correct CNVs regardless of the reference cell type used
2. Separating tumor and normal cells
3. Identifying the right clonality
There are four ways that references can be chosen that deliver equivalent performance when using Numbat, including the Within-dataset, different normal cell types. Our results are based on this mode of reference choice, by using normal cell types found in our own dataset. This mode is recommended over using external-dataset modes, even if the external datasets have matched normal cell types. We had also consulted with the Numbat first author, and their reference choice for their datasets are also from different cell types coming from the same dataset, as their internal experimentations also proved this to be a more effective method. The benchmarking paper recommends this choice above matched normal cell types from external datasets as well.
- External-dataset, matched normal cell types: According to the benchmarking paper, utilizing a within-dataset, different normal cell type is preferred. Additionally, we were unable to find publicly released single-nucleus based RNA ‘normal’ epithelial prostate cells. The released datasets were on single-cell (sc) RNA sequencing, which has a different read- distribution than single-nucleus (sn) RNA sequencing. sn versus sc conducted by the same groups on healthy cells show a moderate difference between the two experimental setups (https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0209648, https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.1011301). Thus, introducing a non-trivial difference in signal due to external datasets. Hence why we chose to use internal-dataset, different cell types.
- External-dataset, different normal cell types: We did not test this as we believe it to not align with neither ours or reviewer’s interest, although this data is reported in the benchmarking paper.
We appreciate the reviewer’s concern in the choice of the reference, as other non-haplotype-dependent CNV inference methods are highly sensitive to the reference choice. However, given the strong evidence from benchmarking papers, our internal experimentation, and consultations with the main Numbat group, and the benchmarking paper, we have adopted a scientifically sound setup for our analyses.
With respect to a more optimized (e.g. Python) implementation of Numbat, we have thoroughly considered it and gone through the entire code-base. To clarify, we previously mentioned that the pairwise distance matrix computation for phylogenetics (ape::nj) grows quadratically with the number of supplied cells. The function’s core is implemented in C++ rather than R, which is significantly faster than both Python and R. Given that the highest performing functions in Python are also C++ based, it is simply a compute limitation despite allocating 2TB of memory. Other parts of Numbat utilize R’s data.table which has a generally faster performance than much of Python’s data processing libraries. Furthermore, according to the benchmarking paper, Numbat’s resource uptake (in memory/GB) is better than most CNV-calling algorithms.
2. While authors do present innovative comparisons through TF motif enrichment, I do not agree that this would remove the need to address biology behind sites through standard approaches. While motif analysis has novelty, results need to be presented and put into context of differential expression (and possibly accessibility) analysis and pathway activation, that I would consider as baseline benchmark for any more complex analysis.
Response: To address the reviewer’s request for a deeper integration of differential gene expression, chromatin accessibility, pathway activity, and TF motif enrichment, we expanded our analyses using SCENIC+ (single-cell enhancer–gene regulatory network) inference (doi:10.1038/s41592-023-01938-4). As now described in the revised Methods section (“Assessing the degree of phenotypic heterogeneity in locus-specific populations,” p. 21, line 31–p. 22, line 4), we applied SCENIC+ to seven tumor samples (ICGC_PCAL34: tumors 1, 2, 4, 10; ICGC_PCAL03: tumors 6, 8, 9).
This algorithm links accessibility, genes, and transcription factors as triplet regulons, and derives the most specific, high-confidence regulons for each cluster. Running this analysis on the seven tumors individually revealed transcription factors and genes specific to low entropy (Fig. 2, Supplementary Fig. 3) malignant epithelial clusters with a sufficient number of cells (N>1000). Since the malignant clusters are specific to each tumor, the high specificity scores of the listed transcription factors and genes for each cluster is representative of intra-tumor heterogeneity (manuscript, newly added Table 2, Cluster_eRegulons). The reported transcription factors by this algorithm include FOX, HOX, FOS/JUN, GRHL, and NR-based TFs.
This reproducibly confirmed our reported sets of TFs driving variance using an orthogonal approach (Fig. 2d, Supplementary Fig. 4).
Given that SCENIC+ also links TFs/accessibility to genes, we also performed pathway enrichment analyses on the lists of genes specific to a given cluster from a tumor (newly added Table 2, Cluster_eRegulons). Performing pathway enrichment analysis on the lists of genes specific to a given cluster, regulated by the reported TFs, revealed distinct and overlapping pathways (FDR < 0.05) (newly added Supplementary Fig. 5, Table 2: Hallmark Pathways). The commonly enriched pathways included androgen and estrogen response, whereas more specific pathways involved EMT, hypoxia, and TGF-β signaling in ICGC_PCAL34, along with p53, TGF-β, PI3K/AKT/mTOR Signaling, mTORC1 and DNA repair pathways in ICGC_PCAL03 (Results, p. 6, line 31-p. 7, line 3).
3. Authors have not properly addressed their claims of plasticity. In my view, raising plasticity as a key concept, will require authors to properly address the transcriptomic (and/or epigenetic) states (and provide definition of cell state) in relation to CNV based clones. Current revision, where non-formal definition of plasticity is given at the end of discussion is far from sufficient.
Response: We thank the reviewer for highlighting the need to better define and contextualize plasticity in relation to transcriptomic and epigenomic states across CNV-defined clones. We have revised the manuscript to more clearly articulate this relationship and to restrain our use of the term plasticity throughout.
While our data, relying on lineage-tracing using CNV-defined clones combined with single-cell RNA and ATAC data from the primary site of tumour development and a secondary site of colonization, supports a role for phenotypic adaptation, we acknowledge the lack of a genetically evolving barcode-based in vitro model that would allow definitive single-cell resolution lineage tracing. Such an approach lies beyond the scope of the present study. Accordingly, we have removed the term “phenotypic plasticity” from the title and all other sections of the manuscript, retaining it only in the discussion when referring to relevant manuscripts by others demonstrating that metastatic potential in prostate cancer can emerge through transcriptional and epigenetic reprogramming rather than de novo clonal selection (manuscript refs 4,6,56–58).
