Recent studies have classified tumors into immune “hot” versus “cold” states based on T cell infiltration, PD-L1 (CD274) expression, and tumor mutational burden (TMB) 30. Prostate cancer is considered an immune-cold tumor type 31, and this is supported by our own single-cell data, where T cells constituted only ~1.95% of all profiled cells, limiting robust T cell-based stratification across patients. With this caveat in mind, we decided to assess CD274 (PD-L1) expression within malignant epithelial cells across tumor and lymph node (LN) foci. Gene expression was log-normalized using the LogNormalize method in Seurat before visualization. Overall, CD274 expression was low across all sites from all patients (Rebuttal Figure 3.7A), consistent with the immune-cold phenotype of prostate cancer.

Reviewer #4, expertise in prostate cancer epigenetics and mechanisms of lineage plasticity (Remarks to the Author):
In this manuscript, Keshavarzian et al employs scMultiome to dissect intra- and inter-tumoral heterogeneity in high-risk prostate cancer across spatially distinct primary tumor loci and matched locoregional lymph node (LN) metastases. This research show that Inter-patient heterogeneity is largely restricted to malignant epithelial cells and LN metastases mirror the clonal diversity of primary tumors but undergo a transcriptional shift toward inflammatory-like states. This work advances the understanding of prostate cancer progression by linking clonal architecture to phenotypic plasticity. The inflammatory transition paradigm also provides a framework for targeting non-genetic adaptation mechanisms in metastasis. The following points need to be considered.
Major comments:
C4.1. The cohort size and clinical annotation are limited in this study which includes only 5 patients, with one receiving neoadjuvant therapy. The author can explicitly discuss how cohort size limits statistical power for inter-patient comparisons and include clinical outcomes (e.g., recurrence, survival) if available to contextualize the observed heterogeneity.
While this study was designed as an in-depth exploratory analysis of spatial heterogeneity using single-cell multiomic profiling in a rare and clinically relevant setting (paired primary and locoregional metastatic tissues from high-risk prostate cancer patients), we agree that a larger cohort size would have been beneficial. Our current cohort includes five patients, the extensive spatial sampling per patient (up to 10 biopsies per individual) and the high resolution of ~300,000 single-nucleus profiles which enabled robust intra-patient comparisons and allowed us to identify conserved phenotypic trends across patients despite inter-individual variation.
Nonetheless, we acknowledge that the small number of patients limits the statistical generalizability of inter-patient comparisons. We now explicitly discuss this limitation in the revised Discussion section and caution against over-interpreting patient-specific findings as broadly representative. Clinical annotations, such as histopathologic features (e.g., Gleason score), were leveraged to contextualize some findings, such as ICGC_PCAL37 in the Results Section “Malignant cells disseminating to locoregional lymph nodes undergo an inflammatory-like cell state transition despite genotypic similarity to primary cancer”; page 9 lines 3-8 and page 10 lines 7-10. Our cohort, which is limited in size and restricted to lymph node metastasis, constraints our ability to expand our findings to distal metastases and contextualize clinical outcomes.
We agree that future studies with larger cohorts and longitudinal follow-up data will be essential to link the observed cellular heterogeneity to patient outcomes and treatment response (raised on page 12, lines 21-25)
C4.2. ICGC_PCAL37, which has the lowest Gleason score, has some specificity in some aspect, such as lower tumor heterogeneity and the unique inter-site difference. These may indicate that the stage of tumor progression can have an impact on the inter- and intra-tumor heterogeneity. The author can discuss how tumor progression relates to the heterogeneity of prostate tumor inter- and intra-site through the analysis of wider range of statistic data from their own or in the public database
Extensive prior work has shown that prostate cancer displays marked inter-patient heterogeneity across histo-morphological and molecular dimensions in both primary and metastatic disease settings 32–37. Large-scale genomic studies have further delineated molecular subtypes of prostate cancer that differ at the genetic level despite sharing similar histopathological grades 38–44.
In our cohort, patient ICGC_PCAL37, the only case with a Gleason score of 7 (3+4), stood out in several respects. This individual exhibited comparatively lower tumor heterogeneity and unique inter-site differences. Clinically, this patient had no evidence of bone metastases (similar to ICGC_PCAL10), experienced biochemical recurrence relatively early, and remained stable for an extended period following salvage radiation therapy before initiating systemic treatment nearly five years later (Table 1: baseline_metadata, therapy_follow_up). These characteristics may reflect a more indolent disease course and support the idea that earlier-stage tumors may harbor lower levels of molecular heterogeneity.
While our dataset includes only five patients, limiting the statistical power to formally compare Gleason score with heterogeneity metrics, previous studies support this link. For example, high-risk prostate cancers with elevated Gleason scores tend to exhibit more pronounced somatic copy number alterations (SCNAs) and greater genomic instability 45, Figure 2). Similarly, The Cancer Genome Atlas44 reported that tumors with high SCNA burden are associated with higher Gleason scores and elevated PSA levels (Figures S3B–S3D).
Furthermore, the degree of structural rearrangement has been shown to increase across Gleason grades: tumors with any Gleason pattern 4 component (e.g., 3+4 or 4+3) demonstrate significantly higher rearrangement rates than Gleason 3+3 tumors 44, Figure 1). These studies collectively support the hypothesis that tumor progression correlates with increasing inter- and intra-tumor heterogeneity.
C4.3. Bone metastases are very common in prostate cancer. Does prostate bone metastases also show an immune/inflammatory-like states transition similar with LN metastases? The author can discuss the potential universality of this inflammatory-like states.
As our cohort includes only lymph node metastases, we are unable to directly assess whether bone metastases exhibit a similar immune/inflammatory-like state transition. However, prior work by others 46 has examined progression biopsies from mCRPC patients, including bone metastases, and similarly reported enrichment of immune/inflammatory-related pathways, such as interferon signaling and IL6/JAK/STAT—during treatment resistance. This suggests that such inflammatory-like states may represent a shared, site-independent mechanism associated with lineage plasticity. While distant metastatic organs such as bone and liver are considered aggressive metastatic disease, locoregional lymph nodes may similarly capture this evolving aggressive biology due to ongoing clonal seeding from the primary site prior to therapy 24. Thus, although our analysis is limited to lymph node metastases, the inflammatory-like transcriptional states we observe may reflect a generalizable mechanism of metastatic adaptation and resistance. sWe have added a brief statement in the Discussion to reflect this point (page 12, lines 3-14): “These immune/inflammatory-like pathways, including JAK-STAT signaling, have also been observed in mCRPC progression samples across diverse metastatic sites, including bone 63. JAK-STAT signalling is also implicated as a driver of plasticity and dedifferentiation from luminal-epithelial cell states in prostate cancer models 64,65. This suggests that activation of these pathways may represent a mechanism of progression and potentially contribute to treatment resistance, though this hypothesis warrants further validation. ”
Lastly, we used our chromatin variants to get their global enrichment over mCRPC bone metastases profiled using bulk ATAC-sequencing. We observed the primary Tu chromatin variants to score lower than the LN chromatin variants (Wilcoxon P=0.008), with respect to the average chromatin accessibility profile across mCPRC samples. However, these samples were profiled using bulk ATAC-sequencing which implies that the computed signal is inclusive of cells in the tumor microenvironment. For this reason, we turned to performing the same analyses on over prostate cancer cell lines which are composed of purely malignant cells. We saw that LN chromatin variants were more enriched in aggressive cell lines (PC3s and Du145, Wilcoxon P=0.029) relative to Tu chromatin variants which were more pronounced in less aggressive hormone dependent cell lines (LNCaP, 22RV1, VCaPs, Wilcoxon P=0.008).
Rebuttal 4.3 LN chromatin variant signatures are more enriched relative to primary Tu in aggressive prostate cancers. A) Chromatin variant enrichments in 28 bulk ATAC-seq mCRPC bone metastasis samples. Enrichment scores computed using ChromVar, which assesses the relative enrichment of all differential LN (N=5544, Log Fold Change > 0.5, adjusted P-val < 0.1) and Tu (N=5312, Log Fold Change > 0.5, adjusted P-val < 0.1) peaks on a consensus mCRPRC peakset. B) Chromatin variant enrichments computed in a similar manner on a consensus cell line peakset, with two replicates per cell line with the exception of VCaPs. C) Depiction of individual cell line data and replicates in (B) as a heatmap, color-scale is limited to a minimum and maximum of -10 and +10 Z-scores.
C4.4. While the transcriptional shifts in LN metastases are compelling, the functional consequences of inflammatory reprogramming remain speculative. In vitro assays (e.g., cytokine exposure) or spatial proteomics could help in validating inflammatory signatures as well as the cellular function of this transition.
While the functional consequences of inflammatory reprogramming remain to be fully elucidated, we partially addressed this by validating our lymph node (LN)-upregulated transcriptional signature using an independent single-cell RNA-seq dataset from metastatic prostate cancer across treatment stages 47. We observed an enrichment of LN-up genes during disease progression and treatment resistance (Figure 4g), supporting their biological relevance. Similar pathways were also shown to be upregulated in mCRPC progression post-Enzalutamide treatment 46, and aggressive prostate cancer cells expressing immune-like markers were previously observed in mouse models 48.
We agree that spatial transcriptomic and proteomic technologies could provide further insight into the local context and function of these states. Similarly recent technological advances, such as spatial scATAC-seq and in situ tagmentation, highlight promising future directions for dissecting spatial epigenomic heterogeneity 49,50.We believe our findings help lay the groundwork for such future studies.
We also acknowledge the potential value of in vitro cytokine exposure assays to interrogate the functional consequences of inflammatory reprogramming. However, given the broad scope of our transcriptional signatures, encompassing multiple pathways and hundreds of genes, designing targeted perturbation experiments would require substantial additional work to deconvolute pathway-specific effects. As with IHC-based validation, these experiments, while valuable, fall beyond the scope of the current study.
C4.5. In this research, sampling focuses on primary tumors and LN metastases but lacks the adjacent normal tissue comparisons to define tumor-specific changes. Spatial transcriptomics may help in mapping phenotypic transitions at the invasion front.
While our manuscript was focused on investigating the primary and metastatic heterogeneity, we did not have access to matched adjacent normals to define tumor-specific changes. However, we utilized the identified tumor-microenvironment cell types as a reference point as discussed in our response to comment C2.7. We have additionally covered how our data highlights spatial transcriptomics to be imperative to our understanding of prostate cancer heterogeneity and metastasis (See response to comment C1.2 and revised Discussion page 11 line 6-20)

Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
The authors have addressed my comments effectively.
Response: Thank you for acknowledging our efforts to address your previous comments effectively, which enabled us to enhance the scientific content of our manuscript.
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
The authors clarified a sufficient amounts of critical points and I am convinced of the robust and rigorous analysis of the data. Maybe, given the lack of further validation that prostate cancer cells converge to a phenotype similar to an inflammatory-like status in the LNs, the title of the manuscript could be slightly modified.
Response: We thank the reviewer for recognizing the rigor and robustness of our work. We have revised the manuscript (title and other sections) as suggested.
Reviewer #4 (Remarks to the Author):
The authors have answered my questions.
Response: Thank you for recognizing the quality and impact of our study.
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
Authors have partially addressed my concerns related to the manuscript. Still major issues remain.
1. For CNV analysis authors could consider more optimized (e.g. python) implementation of the algorithms. None of the less, authors do demonstrate data to alleviate concern regarding subsampling. However, how the choice of reference cell type impacts the CNV calls has not been properly addressed. As different cell types expressed different set of genes this can have fundamental impact on inferred CNVs and thus on conclusions.
Response: We agree with the reviewer that the majority of CNV calling algorithms are based solely on RNA expression and are therefore sensitive to the choice of reference. We did not experience this to be a problem for Numbat because it relies on both haplotype frequency (reference-independent) and molecular abundance (reference-dependent).
To this point, a very recent CNV-calling benchmarking paper showcases that with the exception of Numbat, most other CNV callers are sensitive to the choice of reference (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-62359-9). This paper demonstrated Numbat’s high performance in
1. Outperforming all other methods at detecting the correct CNVs regardless of the reference cell type used
2. Separating tumor and normal cells
3. Identifying the right clonality
There are four ways that references can be chosen that deliver equivalent performance when using Numbat, including the Within-dataset, different normal cell types. Our results are based on this mode of reference choice, by using normal cell types found in our own dataset. This mode is recommended over using external-dataset modes, even if the external datasets have matched normal cell types. We had also consulted with the Numbat first author, and their reference choice for their datasets are also from different cell types coming from the same dataset, as their internal experimentations also proved this to be a more effective method. The benchmarking paper recommends this choice above matched normal cell types from external datasets as well.
- External-dataset, matched normal cell types: According to the benchmarking paper, utilizing a within-dataset, different normal cell type is preferred. Additionally, we were unable to find publicly released single-nucleus based RNA ‘normal’ epithelial prostate cells. The released datasets were on single-cell (sc) RNA sequencing, which has a different read- distribution than single-nucleus (sn) RNA sequencing. sn versus sc conducted by the same groups on healthy cells show a moderate difference between the two experimental setups (https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0209648, https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.1011301). Thus, introducing a non-trivial difference in signal due to external datasets. Hence why we chose to use internal-dataset, different cell types.
- External-dataset, different normal cell types: We did not test this as we believe it to not align with neither ours or reviewer’s interest, although this data is reported in the benchmarking paper.
We appreciate the reviewer’s concern in the choice of the reference, as other non-haplotype-dependent CNV inference methods are highly sensitive to the reference choice. However, given the strong evidence from benchmarking papers, our internal experimentation, and consultations with the main Numbat group, and the benchmarking paper, we have adopted a scientifically sound setup for our analyses.
With respect to a more optimized (e.g. Python) implementation of Numbat, we have thoroughly considered it and gone through the entire code-base. To clarify, we previously mentioned that the pairwise distance matrix computation for phylogenetics (ape::nj) grows quadratically with the number of supplied cells. The function’s core is implemented in C++ rather than R, which is significantly faster than both Python and R. Given that the highest performing functions in Python are also C++ based, it is simply a compute limitation despite allocating 2TB of memory. Other parts of Numbat utilize R’s data.table which has a generally faster performance than much of Python’s data processing libraries. Furthermore, according to the benchmarking paper, Numbat’s resource uptake (in memory/GB) is better than most CNV-calling algorithms.
2. While authors do present innovative comparisons through TF motif enrichment, I do not agree that this would remove the need to address biology behind sites through standard approaches. While motif analysis has novelty, results need to be presented and put into context of differential expression (and possibly accessibility) analysis and pathway activation, that I would consider as baseline benchmark for any more complex analysis.
Response: To address the reviewer’s request for a deeper integration of differential gene expression, chromatin accessibility, pathway activity, and TF motif enrichment, we expanded our analyses using SCENIC+ (single-cell enhancer–gene regulatory network) inference (doi:10.1038/s41592-023-01938-4). As now described in the revised Methods section (“Assessing the degree of phenotypic heterogeneity in locus-specific populations,” p. 21, line 31–p. 22, line 4), we applied SCENIC+ to seven tumor samples (ICGC_PCAL34: tumors 1, 2, 4, 10; ICGC_PCAL03: tumors 6, 8, 9).
This algorithm links accessibility, genes, and transcription factors as triplet regulons, and derives the most specific, high-confidence regulons for each cluster. Running this analysis on the seven tumors individually revealed transcription factors and genes specific to low entropy (Fig. 2, Supplementary Fig. 3) malignant epithelial clusters with a sufficient number of cells (N>1000). Since the malignant clusters are specific to each tumor, the high specificity scores of the listed transcription factors and genes for each cluster is representative of intra-tumor heterogeneity (manuscript, newly added Table 2, Cluster_eRegulons). The reported transcription factors by this algorithm include FOX, HOX, FOS/JUN, GRHL, and NR-based TFs.
This reproducibly confirmed our reported sets of TFs driving variance using an orthogonal approach (Fig. 2d, Supplementary Fig. 4).
Given that SCENIC+ also links TFs/accessibility to genes, we also performed pathway enrichment analyses on the lists of genes specific to a given cluster from a tumor (newly added Table 2, Cluster_eRegulons). Performing pathway enrichment analysis on the lists of genes specific to a given cluster, regulated by the reported TFs, revealed distinct and overlapping pathways (FDR < 0.05) (newly added Supplementary Fig. 5, Table 2: Hallmark Pathways). The commonly enriched pathways included androgen and estrogen response, whereas more specific pathways involved EMT, hypoxia, and TGF-β signaling in ICGC_PCAL34, along with p53, TGF-β, PI3K/AKT/mTOR Signaling, mTORC1 and DNA repair pathways in ICGC_PCAL03 (Results, p. 6, line 31-p. 7, line 3).
3. Authors have not properly addressed their claims of plasticity. In my view, raising plasticity as a key concept, will require authors to properly address the transcriptomic (and/or epigenetic) states (and provide definition of cell state) in relation to CNV based clones. Current revision, where non-formal definition of plasticity is given at the end of discussion is far from sufficient.
Response: We thank the reviewer for highlighting the need to better define and contextualize plasticity in relation to transcriptomic and epigenomic states across CNV-defined clones. We have revised the manuscript to more clearly articulate this relationship and to restrain our use of the term plasticity throughout.
While our data, relying on lineage-tracing using CNV-defined clones combined with single-cell RNA and ATAC data from the primary site of tumour development and a secondary site of colonization, supports a role for phenotypic adaptation, we acknowledge the lack of a genetically evolving barcode-based in vitro model that would allow definitive single-cell resolution lineage tracing. Such an approach lies beyond the scope of the present study. Accordingly, we have removed the term “phenotypic plasticity” from the title and all other sections of the manuscript, retaining it only in the discussion when referring to relevant manuscripts by others demonstrating that metastatic potential in prostate cancer can emerge through transcriptional and epigenetic reprogramming rather than de novo clonal selection (manuscript refs 4,6,56–58).
